anchors.paper_title: The Role of Rapid Eye Movement Sleep in Neural Differentiation of Memories in the Hippocampus
anchors.reason: The dataset README cites this exact paper (McDevitt, Kim, Turk-Browne, Norman, JOCN) as the source of the fMRI and EEG data, with matching title and authors.

metadata.methods_description: Data collection included three fMRI scans and one EEG session per participant. The EEG session recorded either sleep (nap) or quiet wake data depending on the participant's assigned condition. Participants also completed behavioral tasks including a decision task and a reward prediction task during fMRI sessions.

citation_details.title: Adaptive processing of predictions and prediction errors in hippocampal subregions
citation_details.author: Oded Bein, Lila Davachi
citation_details.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
citation_details.abstract: The hippocampus is central to generating memory-based predictions and responding when reality matches or violates these predictions. Here, we examine fMRI research of hippocampal subregions in humans and identify distinct putative mechanisms underlying such predictive processing. Specifically, hippocampal regions CA3 and CA1 may both support predictive processing, but at different stages of learning. Emerging evidence supports the view that CA3 can represent memory-based predictions by pattern-completing the prediction from a cue after only minimal learning. CA1 predictive representations, however, may emerge when predictions are well learnt; CA1, thus, might serve as a 'gatekeeper' that relays established predictions to downstream regions. Through pattern separation, the dentate gyrus may support fine-grained, immediate predictions that distinguish similar events. citation_details.title: Gravity in the Eye: How ‘Gravitational Ischemia’ in the Retina May Be Released and Resolved Through Rapid Eye Movement (REM), a Component of Gravity Opposition Physiology
citation_details.author: J. Howard Jaster, Joshua Ong, Giulia Ottaviani, MD, PhD
citation_details.abstract: In normal terrestrial physiology, the superior retinal hemisphere receives significantly more blood flow than the inferior hemisphere—this includes the influence of the cilioretinal artery (which is congenitally present in 30% of the population), and which significantly localizes to the superior temporal retinal quadrant. This may be an evolutionary adaptation to protect the blood circulation in the superior temporal retinal quadrant, which is exposed to gravitational ischemia during sleep, when the eyes are typically rotated up and out—rolling the superior temporal retinal quadrant into the 'bottom' position, when sleeping in supine position with the nose up. Many of the cardinal features of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome (SANS) may potentially be explained as features of gravity-opposition physiology, which become unopposed by gravity during spaceflight. citation_details.title: Firing Without Wiring: How REM-like Sleep Reactivation Rebalances Excitation and Inhibition to Orthogonalize Memories
citation_details.author: Yoshimasa Kubo, Erik Delanois, Bazhenov Maxim
citation_details.abstract: The role of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation remains poorly understood. Several influential ideas propose that REM sleep serves to eliminate crosstalk between memories, thereby orthogonalizing representations of similar ones; however, mechanistic confirmation remains sparse. Here we used recurrent neural networks trained with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), a biologically plausible training algorithm, to investigate the role of REM-like sleep in memory consolidation. We found that REM-like sleep reduces memory interference by decorrelating task-specific neuronal populations, isolating individual memory traces. During sleep, reactivation was dominated by the population encoding the most recent memory, which had taken over the inputs of older memories during new learning. The excitation/inhibition balance of inputs onto this population shifted toward inhibition, most strongly from older-memory populations, so that older memories again activated their own neurons. citation_details.title: Pre-sleep experiences shape neural activity and dream content in the sleeping brain
citation_details.author: Deniz Kumral, Jessica Palmieri, Steffen Gais, Monika Schönauer
citation_details.abstract: Dreams incorporate recent experiences, and memory-related brain activity is reactivated during sleep, suggesting that dreaming, memory consolidation, and reactivation are tightly linked. We devised a paradigm to investigate whether memory reprocessing during sleep contributes to dreaming. Participants listened to different audiobooks before falling asleep, introducing dissimilar experiences to be processed at night. We show that audiobook content was reprocessed at the neural level using multivariate pattern analyses. Brain activity during rapid eye movement sleep, particularly in the beta range, carried information about the audiobook. While the amount of neural reinstatement did not correlate with memory retention, global beta power during REM sleep was associated with better memory performance. citation_details.title: Imperatorin restores behavioral and recognition memory deficits induced by REM sleep deprivation in male rats
citation_details.author: Mohammad Mojtaba Ayati, M. Eslami, B. G. Yekta
citation_details.abstract: Many studies have shown the deleterious effects of rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep deprivation (SD) on cognitive functions and synaptic plasticity markers. On the other hand, imperatorin (IMP, extracted from the fruits of Angelica dahurica and Peucedanum praeruptorum) may exert significant pro-cognitive and neuroprotective effects. The present study aimed to explore the potential therapeutic effects of IMP on behavioral and molecular changes induced by REM SD, before or after training in the novel object recognition (NOR) memory test. REM SD was done for 24 h and IMP was orally administered at the dose of 100 mg/kg (immediately after REM SD). Locomotion, anxiety-like behavior, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and cAMP response element binding (CREB) levels were also assessed in the prefrontal cortex.
